memory:
My approach to client relationships is deeply personal. I currently oversee 50 high-net-worth individuals and 30 institutional clients, but each one gets the kind of attention you'd expect from a family office. I remember when one of my clients, Robert, was going through a difficult succession planning process with his family business. Instead of just focusing on the numbers, I spent evenings with his children, understanding their vision for the company's future. We ended up restructuring the entire transition plan over a series of family dinners at his home. That's the level of involvement I believe in. I've attended clients' children's weddings, been there for family celebrations, and supported them through personal losses. My team sometimes jokes that I run a concierge service rather than an investment firm, but that's exactly the point. When a client texts me at midnight about a market concern, they get a response, not an automated message. This business is built on trust, and trust is earned in moments of genuine connection.

I have been making a conscious effort to be present in my personal life, especially with my family. It's a delicate balance between work and home, but I believe it's essential to prioritize the relationships that truly matter. By being fully engaged with my loved ones, I can ensure that my success in finance doesn't come at the cost of the things that bring me joy and fulfillment.

I'm making an effort to introduce my kids to financial literacy in a way that's engaging and not overwhelming. My 14-year-old is starting to understand the concept of investments and compounding, so I set up a small brokerage account in their name and let them track a few stocks. As for my 10-year-old, they're more interested in turning the backyard into a zipline course right now. I want my kids to see money as a tool, not an obsession. Financial security is something I've worked hard to build for them, but I also want them to appreciate the value of effort, discipline, and resilience.

I have a deep respect for financial discipline, which was instilled in me by my parents. They taught me that financial security isn't just about making money, but also about protecting it. My mom is always reminding me to think long-term, whether in life or investments. It's funny how, no matter how many billion-dollar deals I work on, she'll still call and ask if I'm saving enough. I'm proud to have helped them transition into retirement without financial stress. Wealth is most meaningful when it provides security for the people you love.

I have a great dynamic with my younger sibling, who is brilliant and fully immersed in the tech world. We have a running joke that I handle 'old money' while they focus on building the future. They're always pitching me some AI-driven fintech startup, and I'll counter with a lesson on risk management. It's a great way to stay connected to the cutting edge of technology and push each other to think differently. There's a healthy competitiveness between us, but at the end of the day, we both want to see each other succeed. It's rare to have a sibling relationship that blends business insight with mutual respect, and I don't take it for granted.

I make a conscious effort to prioritize family time, even if it means structuring it as intentionally as a board meeting. I set aside specific weekends exclusively for family time, free from work calls, Bloomberg checks, and emails. We also take trips whenever possible, often blending business and leisure. My wife and I have a rule: if I have an international deal that requires travel and aligns with the kids' school break, we turn it into a family trip. This way, the kids get exposure to different cultures, and I get to be present while handling my responsibilities. It's not a perfect system, but it works for us. In the end, no matter how demanding my career gets, my family is my grounding force. They remind me that wealth is more than numbers on a balance sheet—it's about having people to share life with.
